background.definition: Folliculitis is defined as inflammation of hair follicles due to infectious and non-infectious causes and presents as erythematous papules and pustules centered around hair follicles. Folliculitis affects the superficial hair follicle, whereas a furuncle involves the deep hair follicle.

list.listitem: The incidence of folliculitis is unknown but thought to be common. Patients often do not present to physicians because the disease is usually self-limited.

Folliculitis is due to infectious and non-infectious causes. Infectious causes include bacterial, fungal, viral, and parasitic. Non-infectious etiologies include folliculitis decalvans and eosinophilic folliculitis. A 6-year prospective study of 240 cases of folliculitis at a Turkish academic medical center found an infectious etiology in 90% of cases (34% fungal, 29% parasitic, 24% bacterial, 3% viral). Non-infectious folliculitis only accounted for 10% of cases. However, disease in this referral population is likely not reflective of folliculitis in the primary care setting.

Staphylococcus aureus and beta-hemolytic Streptococcus are common gram-positive bacterial pathogens. Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a gram-negative bacteria in contaminated water, has been implicated in "hot-tub" folliculitis. Other gram-negative organisms include Klebsiella, Enterobacter, and Proteus spp. In the Turkish trial, S. aureus accounted for 96.5% of bacterial folliculitis, whereas P. aeruginosa made up only 3.5% of bacterial cases.
Fungal pathogens include Candida sp., Malassezia sp. (Malassezia folliculitis), and dermatophytes.
Viruses that have been isolated include herpes simplex virus (HSV folliculitis), varicella zoster virus (VZV folliculitis), and DNA poxvirus (molluscum folliculitis).
Parasitic causes included Sarcoptes scabiei (scabies folliculitis) and Demodex mite (Demodex folliculitis).
Folliculitis decalvans or tufted folliculitis is an uncommon neutrophilic scarring alopecia of unclear etiology, but is thought to be triggered by immunologic alteration and presence of Staph aureus.
Eosinophilic pustular folliculitis (EPF) is a sterile papulopustular follicular eruption of unknown etiology.

In HIV patients with pruritic folliculitis, the predominant lesion was EPF (45%), followed by bacterial folliculitis (41%), and Pityrosporum folliculitis (10%) based on characteristic histopathological features from skin biopsies.

Folliculitis is the most common reported adverse effect of epidermal growth factor receptor inhibitors (EGFRIs) used for treatment of lung, gastrointestinal, and head and neck malignancies. Other medications that have been implicated in acneiform, but not necessarily follicular, eruptions include corticosteroids, anabolic steroids, testosterone, antidepressants, antipsychotics, anticonvulsants, cyclosporine, azathioprine, tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha) inhibitors, antituberculosis drugs, quinidine, and danazol.
Folliculitis results from superficial inflammation of hair follicles, often due to an infectious cause.
Skin trauma or occlusion often precedes the infection.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Skin occlusion or aggressive use of topical ointments, creams, makeup, or steroids
Contaminated or heated water (e.g., whirlpools, swimming pools, hot tubs )
Diabetes, HIV, and other forms of immunodeficiency

list.listitem: Suspect folliculitis in patients presenting with erythematous, follicularly-centered papules and pustules of the scalp, face, chest, back, axilla, thigh, buttocks, and groin.

If available, perform dermoscopy when folliculitis is suspected. Dermoscopy can help differentiate folliculitis from pseudofolliculitis and other nonfollicular pustular disorders. A 6-year observational study of 240 consecutive patients in Turkey reported the overall diagnostic accuracy of dermoscopy in identifying folliculitis as 73.7%, with a diagnostic accuracy of 100% for dermatophytes, 89.7% for scabies, 88.1% for Demodex, and 92.8% for pseudofolliculitis. However, dermoscopy's diagnostic accuracy to identify Staphylococal folliculitis was low (50.9%).

Folliculitis, on dermoscopy, presents as follicular erythematous papulopustules, whereas pseudofolliculitis demonstrates U-shaped ingrowing hairs. Nonfollicular pustular disorders do not clearly demonstrate hair at the center of the papulopustule.
Staphylococcal folliculitis typically does not cause pain or systemic toxicity but may cause itching. Crusting, variably, may be present.
Consider methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) if folliculitis is refractory to treatment or distributed along the chest, flank, periumbilical, and scrotal areas.
A furuncle, a deeper form of folliculitis, presents as a small, erythematous, warm, tender, subcutaneous nodule or fluctuant cyst, often with a superficial pustule.

Pseudomonas folliculitis, due to hot tubs or whirlpools, appears 6 to 72 hours after exposure and usually resolves spontaneously in 7 to 10 days. Lesions appear as urticarial follicular papulopustules, may have pronounced peripheral erythema, and are distributed along the buttocks, flanks, and hips. The face, palms, and soles are usually spared. "Hot tub" folliculitis may present with fever, headache, malaise, and gastrointestinal symptoms.
Malassezia folliculitis occurs in the same cape distribution as tinea versicolor and is caused by the same Malassezia organisms.
Demodex folliculitis or rosacealike demodicosis is a follicular papulopustular eruption that affects the face, perioral, and periauricular areas.
Folliculitis decalvans is a scarring alopecia that presents as perifollicular erythema, scaling, crusting, pustules, and tufted hairs (dolly hairs or polytrichia).

Classic epithelial pustular folliculitis (EPF) or Ofuji disease affects immunocompetent patients and presents as pruritic, urticarial, follicular papulopustules on the trunk, extremities, and face. It resolves spontaneously but may cause post-inflammatory dyspigmentation. Other variants include immunosuppression-associated EPF (very pruritic and affects HIV patients), infantile EPF (affects scalp), and episodic EPF (predilection for face).

Pseudofolliculitis is not true folliculitis. The most common clinical presentation is pseudofolliculitis barbae, which manifests as inflammatory papules of the cheeks and neck, in response to U-shaped ingrowing hairs puncturing adjacent skin on reentry. It is common among African-American males who shave, but also affects women who pluck or shave hair.

If diagnosis of folliculitis is unclear after obtaining a detalied history and thorough physical exam with or without dermoscopy, consider cytologic evaluation, culture, or histopathologic evaluation.

Cytologic evaluation of skin scraping may be helpful in identifying various infectious causes. Obtain skin scraping of papulopustule on a glass slide and consider different staining techniques. Potassium hydroxide exam is useful in identifying fungal folliculitis and may reveal blastospores and pseudohyphae (Candidal folliculitis), hyphae and spores (dermatophytic folliculitis), and budding spores (Malassezia folliculitis). Gram stain helps identify bacterial folliculitis, while Giemsa stain is useful for diagnosing parasites like S. scabiei and Demodex mite.

If folliculitis is unresponsive to treatment and bacterial cause, espcially CA-MRSA, is suspected, consider performing culture by prepping area with chlorhexidine, then scraping off an entire pustule with a sterile No. 15 blade, and depositing the material onto the tip of cotton swab of the transport media.

A 4-mm punch biopsy around a pustular follicle (or other primary lesion) can determine if the predominant organisms are bacterial or fungal. Histopathologic evaluation is also an accurate way to make the diagnosis of EPF. Biopsy may also pick up other dermatologic diagnoses not initially considered and may in fact rule out the diagnosis of folliculitis.

When herpes simplex or herpes zoster folliculitis is suspected and diagnostic certainty needs to be established, consider performing polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test on one or a few pustules after unroofing them, or on any open lesions.
Obtain a detailed history looking for associated symptoms like pruritus, systemic symptoms, precipitating factors, past medical and family history, exposures, and a careful medication review.

Perform a thorough physical exam looking at lesion size, uniformity, distribution, and presence of secondary skin changes like scale, crust, scarring, and alopecia. Augment your clinical exam by performing dermoscopy, if available, to ascertain the follicular nature of lesions, which differentiates folliculitis from pseudofolliculitis and other nonfollicular pustular dermatoses. Dermoscopy is not helpful in diagnosing bacterial folliculitis, but with appropriate training has high diagnostic accuracy in identifiying scabietic folliculitis, Demodex folliculitis, and dermatophytic folliculitis.
Culturing the lesions is not necessary for most patients. Cultures can be considered for lesions that fail to respond to conservative measures.

A small retrospective Japanese study recommends performing culture in cases of late-phase EGFRI-induced folliculitis (>4 weeks post-initiation) given the high rate of staphylococcal antibiotic resistance. Early-phase EGFRI-induced folliculitis, which begins around the first to second week of treatment and disappers after four weeks, can be managed expectantly.
Patients with mild disease do not require antibiotics, which should be reserved for patients with resistant cases or extensive skin involvement.

Consider performing biopsy in patients with unclear diagnosis despite performance of cytologic evaluation, those who are unresponsive to empiric antibiotics for presumed bacterial folliculitis, or when considering initiating systemic antifungal therapy.
First-line treatment for mild disease is antibacterial soaps, and the elimination of predisposing factors such as occlusion, moisture, and abrasion.C
For localized but refractory bacterial folliculitis, consider mupirocin ointment.C
Treat extensive bacterial folliculitis with oral antibiotics effective for methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA), such as cephalexin and dicloxacillin.C
Evaluate refractory bacterial folliculitis for community-acquired methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (CA-MRSA) and treat with doxycycline or trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole.C

Pseudomonas folliculitis should not be treated with topical or systemic antibiotics unless the infection is persistent or the patient is immunocompromised, in which case a fluoroquinolone may be used.C

For mild disease, antibacterial soaps may be the only treatment needed. The skin should be kept dry and friction should be avoided. Predisposing factors (occlusion, moisture, abrasion) should be eliminated if possible.
For localized refractory lesions, consider topical mupirocin ointment.
For extensive skin involvement, cephalexin or dicloxacillin may be used. Although CA-MRSA is prevalent in many communities, initial therapy should be directed at MSSA.
For refractory bacterial folliculitis, culture for CA-MRSA and treat with doxycycline or trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole.

Pseudomonas folliculitis generally resolves spontaneously in 7 to 10 days without antibiotics. If the patient is immunocompromised or the lesions are persistent, oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg every 12 hours for 10 to 14 days may be used. Pseudomonas folliculitis can be prevented by adequate chlorination of whirlpools and hot tubs and by periodically changing the water.
A Cochrane review did not identify any randomized controlled trials to examine the efficacy and safety of topical antibiotics compared with systemic antibiotics for treating bacterial folliculitis.

Malassezia folliculitis: Danish guidelines point out that systemic antifungals are more effective than topical antifungals but suggest combination therapy may be more advantageous. Combination therapy using systemic and topical antifungals may shorten duration of treatment.
Herpetic folliculitis: Acyclovir, valacyclovir, or famciclovir can be used.

Demodex folliculitis: Treatments include topical permethrin, crotamiton,and benzyl benzoate, as well as oral metronidazole. Topical ivermectin 1% applied daily for 16 weeks appears effective in eradicating Demodex mites and in decreasing inflammatory lesions from papulopustular rosacea of any severity.

Scabies folliculitis: This is treated like typical scabies, using topical permethrin or, alternatively, systemic or topical ivermectin. Patient and household contacts require treatment, including decontamination of clothing and personal items.

Eosinophilic pustular folliculitis: First-line treatment for eosinophilic pustular folliculitis (EPF) is topical corticosteroids and topical calcineurin inhibitors. Oral indomethacin (50-75 mg/day) may be used cautiously, given its gastrointestinal side effects. For HIV-associated EPF refractory to topical steroids and indomethacin, consider high-dose cetirizine, oral metronidazole, systemic itraconazole, and topical permethrin. UVB phototherapy is another option.

Epitheleal growth factor receptor inhibitor (EGFRI)-induced folliculitis: Based on weak evidence, EGFRI-induced folliculitis may be prevented using prophylactic use of tetracycline. The rash gradually disappears afte stopping EGFRI use.
Folliculitis decalvans: This can be treated with rifampin plus clindamycin, tetracyclines, and intralesional steroids.

Pseudofolliculitis barbae: This conditions is treated by minimizing trauma during hair removal. Pharmacological treatment options include low-potency corticosteroids, benzoyl peroxide, antibiotics, and retinoids. Adjustable razors or chemical depilatories can be used for men who must shave.
Referral to a dermatologist is rarely indicated but may be necessary if the lesions are refractory or the diagnosis is unclear.
Folliculitis usually resolves without scarring following conservative treatment. C
The need for follow-up will depend on the severity and extent of the lesions. C
